topic: Privacy-First Contact Tracing: The DP-3T Algorithm
target_audience: University students in Computer Science or Data Privacy

outline.topic: Privacy-First Contact Tracing: The DP-3T Algorithm
outline.target_audience: University students in Computer Science or Data Privacy

sections.title: The Privacy-Security Paradox
sections.content: Introduction to the challenge: How do we track disease spread without creating a 'Big Brother' surveillance state? Prerequisite: Understanding basic client-server architecture and the difference between centralized vs. decentralized data storage.
sections.example: Imagine two robots, 'Pixel' and 'Nexus', meeting in a park. They want to remember they met in case one gets 'rusty' (infected), but they don't want to tell a central computer their names or locations.

sections.title: Generating Digital Disguises (Ephemeral IDs)
sections.content: Explanation of how a phone generates a daily 'Secret Key' (SK) and then uses a Hash Function H(SK) to create thousands of 'Ephemeral IDs' (EphIDs) that rotate every 15 minutes. Visual: A rotating wheel of random numbers derived from one seed.
sections.example: Pixel's phone generates a Secret Key 'K_p'. Every 15 minutes, it creates a new temporary ID: EphID_1 = Hash(K_p, 9:00), EphID_2 = Hash(K_p, 9:15). To a bystander, Pixel looks like a different person every 15 minutes.

sections.title: The Invisible Handshake (BLE Exchange)
sections.content: Mechanics of Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) chirps. When two devices are close, they exchange their current EphIDs and store them locally. Key concept: The server is NOT involved in this exchange. Visual: Two phones emitting colorful 'ripples' of random numbers toward each other.
sections.example: When Nexus and Pixel stand within 2 meters, Nexus's phone hears 'EphID_88' from Pixel and saves it in its local 'Seen Diary'. Pixel's phone does the same for Nexus.

sections.title: The Diagnosis Report (Infection Event)
sections.content: When a user is diagnosed, they voluntarily upload their 'Daily Secret Keys' (not their identities or locations) to a central bulletin board. Visual: A public chalkboard where a sick robot writes only their 'Secret Seed' for the days they were contagious.
sections.example: Pixel tests positive. He uploads his Secret Key 'K_p' for Monday to the server. The server now hosts a list of keys belonging to 'Infected' users, but it still doesn't know Pixel's name.

sections.title: Local Matching: The Final Privacy Shield
sections.content: Every phone periodically downloads the list of 'Infected Secret Keys' from the server. The phone locally regenerates the possible EphIDs from those keys and checks for a match in its own 'Seen Diary'. Math concept: Intersection of sets A (Seen IDs) and B (Regenerated Infected IDs).
sections.example: Nexus's phone downloads Pixel's Secret Key. It runs the Hash function locally: 'If I saw EphID_88, and this Secret Key generates EphID_88, then I was near a sick person!' Nexus receives a notification, but the server never knows Nexus was the one who checked.

storyboard.title: The Privacy-Security Paradox
lecture_lines: Traditional contact tracing often relies on central surveillance.
This risks exposing sensitive user location and identity.
DP-3T provides a decentralized, privacy-first alternative approach.
animations: Fade in a red virus icon (#FF5555) on the left and a green shield icon (#55FF55) on the right to represent the tension between health and privacy.
Create a central white server icon (#FFFFFF) in the middle with multiple grey phone icons (#AAAAAA) around it, connecting them with thin red lines to symbolize centralized tracking.
Remove the central server and connect the grey phone icons (#AAAAAA) directly to each other with thin blue lines (#5555FF) to represent the decentralized DP-3T approach.

storyboard.title: Generating Digital Disguises (Ephemeral IDs)
lecture_lines: Each phone generates a daily Secret Key (SK).
A cryptographic hash function transforms this Secret Key.
This creates thousands of temporary Ephemeral IDs.
IDs rotate every fifteen minutes to prevent tracking.
To others, the user appears as a new person.
animations: Display a bold blue text 'Secret Key (SK)' (#5555FF) at the top of the screen next to a phone icon.
Place a grey gear icon (#888888) in the center labeled 'Hash Function' with an arrow pointing from the Secret Key into it.
Show a sequence of yellow text IDs 'EphID_1', 'EphID_2', 'EphID_3' (#FFFF55) emerging from the gear one after another.
Add a rotating yellow clock icon (#FFFF55) and change the active 'EphID' text color to cyan (#00FFFF) every time the clock completes a rotation.
Add a grey 'Bystander' icon (#CCCCCC) on the side with a question mark bubble, showing that they see the different IDs but cannot link them together.

storyboard.title: The Invisible Handshake (BLE Exchange)
lecture_lines: Nearby phones exchange Ephemeral IDs using Bluetooth.
This "handshake" happens locally between the two devices.
No central server is involved in this exchange.
Each phone stores a "diary" of seen IDs.
These logs remain strictly on the user's device.
animations: Place two grey phone icons (#AAAAAA) labeled 'Pixel' and 'Nexus' on opposite sides of the screen.
Animate cyan concentric ripples (#00FFFF) moving from 'Pixel' to 'Nexus', carrying a small text label 'EphID_88'.
Display a white 'Seen Diary' box (#FFFFFF) next to 'Nexus' and show the label 'EphID_88' moving inside the box and staying there.

storyboard.title: The Diagnosis Report (Infection Event)
lecture_lines: Infected users voluntarily upload their daily Secret Keys.
Only the keys are shared, never their identities.
A central bulletin board hosts these infected keys.
animations: Change the color of 'Pixel's' phone icon to red (#FF0000) to indicate a positive diagnosis.
Draw a white 'Bulletin Board' rectangle (#FFFFFF) on the right side of the screen.
Animate a blue 'Secret Key' label (#5555FF) moving from Pixel's phone to the Bulletin Board.
Display a red 'X' over the words 'Name' and 'Location' (#FF0000) near the moving Secret Key to show they are not shared.
Populate the Bulletin Board with a list of multiple blue labels (#5555FF) representing keys from other infected users.

storyboard.title: Local Matching: The Final Privacy Shield
lecture_lines: Phones periodically download the list of infected keys.
Each phone locally regenerates the corresponding Ephemeral IDs.
It checks for matches within its own seen diary.
Matching occurs privately without notifying the central server.
Users get alerts while maintaining total digital anonymity.
animations: Animate the list of blue keys (#5555FF) moving from the Bulletin Board down to 'Nexus's' phone.
Show a small grey gear (#888888) inside Nexus's phone spinning to generate a set of IDs (Set B) from the downloaded keys.
Display the 'Seen Diary' (Set A) next to the phone, containing IDs like 'EphID_88'.
Flash a bright yellow highlight (#FFFF00) over the matching ID 'EphID_88' found in both the Seen Diary and the generated set.
Popup a cyan 'Notification' bubble (#00FFFF) above Nexus's phone with the text 'Exposure Detected'.
